plot_extraction.response_text:
After years of wandering, the aging poet Owen Hanrahan settles in an abandoned cabin and supports himself by teaching local children. Returning from a night away, he meets Nora, a young woman being forced to marry the wealthy, elderly Paddy Doe. She asks Hanrahan to shame Paddy with a satirical song. When Nora casually says Paddy is as old as Hanrahan, the poet is devastated by the realization that others now see him as an old man.

Angry at age, decay, and his fading appeal, Hanrahan composes a curse against ancient creatures, local old men, and especially Paddy Doe, while blessing May blossoms because they die in their beauty. He teaches the song to his pupils and sends them across the countryside to spread it. The insult soon provokes a mob of old men, led by those named in the song, who march on his cabin with sticks. Hanrahan flees, then watches them set fire to his home. Having turned old age itself against him, he is forced to become a wanderer once more.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the manner of an orally transmitted Irish folk tale, combining plain rural storytelling with mythic suggestion and lyrical symbolism. Its third-person narrator remains close to Hanrahan’s thoughts while retaining the authority of a traditional storyteller who knows his history, reputation, and supernatural entanglements. Repeated connective openings such as “And,” “But,” and “For” create a cumulative, spoken cadence, as though the narrative were being recited aloud. Time is loosely legendary rather than precisely historical, while named villages, mountains, lakes, holy days, and local families give the tale a strongly rooted sense of place.

The diction is simple, archaic, and Hiberno-English in flavour. Constructions such as “it is I know,” “what is on you,” “let you make no delay,” and “it was not long till” reproduce Irish speech patterns without making the prose difficult to follow. Formal or elevated phrases—“to the end of life and time,” “the power of the curse-making bards,” and “O Blessed Queen of Heaven”—sit beside homely details such as eggs, oaten cake, turf, sour milk, sacks, thatch, and blackthorn sticks. This mixture makes the everyday countryside feel continuous with legend, poetry, religion, and magic.

The syntax tends toward long, flowing sentences made from linked clauses. These clauses often accumulate through repetition, especially with “and,” allowing memories, physical details, and emotional associations to gather gradually. Shorter statements and exclamations then mark moments of shock or comic emphasis. Dialogue is direct and ceremonious, with speakers frequently repeating names and claims, and Hanrahan’s speech is especially expansive and self-dramatising. He speaks of personal troubles in the language of poets, queens, curses, and world history, which gives him dignity while also exposing his vanity.

Imagery is seasonal and symbolic. White hawthorn, birdsong, May blossom, wind, old trees, an ancient eagle, and a long-lived pike connect human life to the natural world. Youth is figured as blossom: fresh, white, beautiful, and destined to disappear before decay can touch it. Old age is represented through greyness, stiffness, gaps, hooks, aches, crooked limbs, and withering. The story repeatedly contrasts May’s fertility and beauty with bodily decline. The hare crossing Hanrahan’s path functions as a folkloric omen, and the landscape itself seems populated by powers capable of guiding, warning, or persecuting him.

The emotional register blends melancholy, grandeur, irony, and broad comedy. Hanrahan’s recognition of ageing is genuinely painful, conveyed through memories of social neglect and an increasingly unsparing catalogue of bodily decline. Yet his response is absurdly disproportionate: wounded by a girl’s casual comparison, he curses old age and recruits schoolchildren to spread the insult throughout the district. The old men’s retaliatory march, armed with sticks and moving like a storm, turns his poetic campaign into physical farce. The humour does not erase the sadness; rather, both arise from the same conflict between Hanrahan’s heroic self-image and his vulnerable, ageing body.

Characterisation is achieved through action, remembered reputation, and stylised speech rather than psychological analysis. Hanrahan appears as a wandering poet, teacher, flatterer, lover, and supposed possessor of bardic power. He is charismatic and imaginative but also vain, impulsive, and blind to the consequences of his words. His status is ambiguous: the community tolerates his wandering because he is a poet, yet it can quickly turn against him when his art becomes malicious. The children form a mischievous chorus that converts private resentment into public song, while the old men become both comic individuals and allegorical embodiments of “Old Age and Time and Weariness and Sickness.”

The narrative structure is circular and ironic. It begins with Hanrahan apparently settled after years of wandering, introduces an omen, then uses a small personal wound to provoke the act that destroys his new stability. His curse is effective in spreading through the countryside, but its practical effect is not the defeat of old age or Paddy Doe; it is the burning of Hanrahan’s cabin and his return to homelessness. Thus poetic power is presented as real in social terms—songs travel, shape reputations, and mobilise people—but unreliable and self-destructive when driven by pride.

The inset poem formalises the story’s central oppositions. Its rhyming couplets, repeated curses, catalogue of aged figures, and final blessing on the May blossom resemble a public bardic satire adapted into a memorable street song. The regular rhyme and list structure make it easy for children and beggars to transmit, showing poetry as communal and performative rather than private. The prose surrounding it repeatedly stresses recitation, memorisation, tunes, and circulation, reinforcing the story’s oral aesthetic.

Overall, the style is folkloric, lyrical, locally grounded, and gently tragicomic. It elevates an ordinary episode of wounded vanity into a symbolic confrontation between poetry and time, while allowing the final image of the fleeing poet and the burning thatch to puncture his grand rhetoric. The closing prayer gathers natural emblems and angry villagers into one imaginative category, ending on a characteristic fusion of mythic fear, self-pity, wit, and rueful acceptance.

### Hanrahan’s Song Against Age

It was after many years of roads and fairs and wakes, and sleeping under hedges or in the lofts of friendly houses, that Owen Hanrahan came to a little empty cabin between Ballygawley and the foot of Slieve Daeane. There was a roof of black thatch on it, though the rain came through in two places, and there was a hearth, and a stool with three legs, and a patch of ground where nettles and dock leaves had taken possession.

And Hanrahan said, “It is enough for a man that has followed queens in dreams and women in the world, and has had neither thanks nor peace from the one or the other.”

He cut the nettles, stopped the holes with rushes and clay, and borrowed a pot from a widow. The people brought him turf, eggs, oaten cake, and sometimes a cup of sour milk. In return he gathered the children into the cabin and taught them their letters, and the histories of Cuchulain and Finn, and a little Latin he had kept from his young days. But he taught them more songs than prayers, and more of the doings of poets than of kings; for it is I know he believed a poet’s word would outlast a king’s stone house.

So the seasons went over him quietly. He had a bed of heather in the corner, a brown hen scratching at the threshold, and smoke rising from his roof in the evenings. And some said wandering Hanrahan was settled at last.

But there is no settled place for a man whose pride is quicker than his judgment.

On the night before May Day he went to a house beyond Collooney, where there was music and dancing, and where they had asked him to make verses for a wedding. He stayed until the candles were gutters of wax and the young people had gone out under the whitening sky. It was near sunrise when he took the mountain road home, his coat about him and his head heavy with drink and remembrance.

The hawthorn was white along the ditches, and birds were calling from every little wood, and the grass had the shining greenness that comes only once in the year. Yet Hanrahan noticed none of these things, for he was thinking of a girl with yellow hair who had danced with every young farmer in the house and had not once looked toward him.

A hare ran across the road before his feet and stopped upon a bank. It looked back at him with one dark eye.

“Go your way,” said Hanrahan. “I have followed your kind before, and little good came of it.”

The hare went into the hazels, but he heard a laugh where it had vanished, or thought he heard one, and this left an uneasiness upon him.

It was not long till he came to a well under an old ash tree, and there he saw a young woman sitting with her shawl drawn over her head. She was crying, but when she heard his step she dried her eyes and stood up.

“Good morrow, Owen Hanrahan,” she said.

“Good morrow, Nora Burke,” said he, for he knew her family. “And what sorrow is on you at the beginning of May, when sorrow should be shut in the house and gladness walking the roads?”

“My father will have me married to Paddy Doe of Knocknaroy,” she said. “He has cattle in three fields, and money put away, and a slated house. My father says a full haggard is better than a handsome face.”

“And is Paddy Doe hateful to you?”

“He is stiff in the knees and grey in the beard. His breath whistles, and he counts every potato put into the pot. He has buried two wives, and maybe it is a third grave he is wanting filled.”

Hanrahan lifted his head, for there was nothing he liked better than being called to defend beauty against wealth.

“O Nora Burke,” he said, “there were women before you that were sold for cattle, and kingdoms went down because of it. Helen was carried over the sea, and Deirdre’s sorrow reddened the swords of Ulster. Let your father make no delay in hearing this: gold can buy a roof, but it cannot buy the month of May.”

“It is a song I want from you,” said Nora. “Make a song that will put shame on Paddy Doe, and the boys will sing it at the fair. Then maybe he will leave me in peace.”

“That I will do,” said Hanrahan. “I will make such a song as will loosen the slates on his house and turn his cattle’s faces from him. The curse-making bards had power to raise blemishes on kings, and there is some spark of that power in me yet.”

Nora smiled through her tears. “You will know well what to say of an old man, Hanrahan, being near his age yourself.”

There was no more malice in her words than there is in a bird picking a seed from the road. But Hanrahan stood as if she had struck him.

“Near his age?” he said.

“Indeed, I meant no offence.”

“Paddy Doe is an old stump with moss on him.”

“He is not so much older than yourself, maybe.”

Hanrahan turned from her and looked into the well. There was his own face trembling in the water, lined about the eyes, the beard mixed with grey, the cheeks fallen in from what they had been. He put up his hand and felt the loose skin beneath his chin.

And all at once many small things came into his mind: how girls no longer made room for him beside the fire; how married women called him “poor Hanrahan” and gave him food; how young men listened to his songs but laughed when he spoke of love; how his back ached after a night on hard ground; and how, that very morning, the yellow-haired girl had passed him as if he were a gatepost.

“Nora Burke,” he said, and his voice was low, “there was a time women did not speak to me of age.”

“I ask your pardon,” she said. “It was thoughtless talk.”

But he went by her without farewell, and all the whiteness of the hawthorn seemed an insult to him.

When he came to his cabin the children were waiting, seven or eight of them, with books under their arms and mischief in their eyes. Hanrahan sent them away, saying there would be no schooling until the next day. Then he shut the door and sat before the cold hearth.

He thought of the eagle that had lived since before the saints came into Ireland, its feathers dropping one by one upon a bare mountain. He thought of the pike in Lough Gara, long as a man’s arm and scarred with years, lying among weeds in the dark water. He thought of old yew trees twisted over churchyards, and of ravens croaking on ruined towers.

“Why should anything live beyond its beauty?” he cried. “What right has Time to leave the husk when the grain is gone?”

He walked up and down the narrow floor, naming every old man he disliked and every ache he feared. There was Paddy Doe with his buried wives; Mat Hession, whose nose had a drop forever hanging from it; Darby Flynn, bent double over his stick; and old Shawn Grogan, who had three teeth and used them all for gossip.

And because anger is a strong wind in the house of poetry, the words began coming to him. He wrote them with a burned stick upon the whitewashed wall when paper failed him, and before noon he had made a song.

The next day he called the children in. He stood before them with his coat buttoned and his hair combed back, as solemn as a priest at Mass.

“Listen now,” he said, “and keep every word, for this is a judgment on Age, and Weariness, and the greedy hand that would lay winter upon spring.”

Then he sang:

> A curse on the eagle that moults on the stone,  
> And counts all the kingdoms that wither and groan;  
> A curse on the pike in the cold reedy mere,  
> That has swallowed young fishes a hundredth year.  
>   
> A curse upon Darby, bent down like a bow,  
> And Mat with the winter hung under his brow;  
> On Grogan, whose teeth are but three in a row,  
> And twice seven curses on old Paddy Doe.  
>   
> His knee gives a crack and his shoulder a sting,  
> Yet he reaches a claw for the youth of the spring;  
> May his money grow mould and his chimney smoke low,  
> And no girl share the blanket of old Paddy Doe.  
>   
> But a blessing on blossom that whitens the spray,  
> For it dies in its beauty at ending of May;  
> No wrinkle can touch it, no cold blood can slow—  
> God shelter the blossom from old Paddy Doe.

The children were silent for the length of a breath, and then they shouted with laughter. Before an hour had passed they knew the song better than their alphabet.

“Go east and west with it,” said Hanrahan. “Sing it at the crossroads and beside the wells. Give it to every beggar and cattle-driver between Tubbercurry and Ballysadare. And if any man asks where it came from, say Owen Hanrahan made it by the authority of poets.”

They went like starlings let loose from a barn.

By evening the boys minding cows were singing the second verse. By the next day it was heard at the forge, and the blacksmith beat time to it on the anvil. A blind fiddler carried it to the market. Women sang the blessing on the blossom while washing clothes in the river, and young fellows added verses concerning Paddy Doe’s bald head and the squeaking of his boots.

Nora’s father heard it and swore. Paddy Doe heard it and swore longer.

But it was not Paddy alone who felt the hook. Darby Flynn’s grandchildren sang the verse outside his door. Someone chalked an eagle upon Mat Hession’s gate. Shawn Grogan found three white pebbles set upon his window ledge, in remembrance of his teeth. And every grey head in the district began to think Hanrahan’s song had been aimed at him.

On the third evening a little boy came running to the cabin.

“They are coming, Master Hanrahan!”

“Who is coming?”

“All the old men.”

Hanrahan went to the door. Along the road, under a sky red with sunset, there came a company of men with sticks. Paddy Doe was at their head in a tall hat, carrying a blackthorn knobbed like a bishop’s crozier. Behind him limped Darby Flynn, Mat Hession, Shawn Grogan, and a score more from scattered farms, some bent, some stiff, some coughing, but every one driven onward by rage.

There were bald heads, white whiskers, watery eyes, hooked shoulders, swollen knuckles, and legs that went unwillingly beneath them. Yet as Hanrahan watched, they seemed to grow beyond themselves. They were no longer merely neighbours he had mocked. They were Old Age and Time and Weariness and Sickness, marching together to claim him.

He barred the door and looked about for a weapon. There was only the school rod, the pot, and a sod of turf.

Then a stone struck the wall.

“Come out, curse-maker!” cried Paddy Doe.

“Come out till we teach you respect for your elders!” shouted Grogan.

“I respect elders that have wisdom,” Hanrahan called through the door, “but not withered hands reaching for young women.”

A roar answered him, and the door shook beneath the first blow of a stick.

Hanrahan remembered the back window, little more than a hole where the clay had fallen away. He pushed through it, tearing his coat, and ran into the field. A child saw him and gave a warning cry, but by then he was over the ditch and among the hazels.

From there he looked back.

The old men broke open the door. They dragged out his stool, his heather bed, his books, and the little board on which the children wrote their letters. Paddy Doe kicked apart the hearth. Then Mat Hession thrust a burning wisp of straw beneath the thatch.

The flame went slowly at first, blue and uncertain. But the evening wind took it, and in a moment the roof was red. Sparks rose among the May branches, and the hen flew squawking from the smoke. The children cheered until they remembered it was Hanrahan’s home, and then some began to cry.

He stood hidden while the walls blackened and the roof fell inward. All his settlement, his school, his pot, his poor bed, and the little peace he had gathered after so many roads went up together into the darkening sky.

And he thought, “My song has power indeed, for it has brought all Age against me; but it had not the wisdom to tell me I was inside the thing I cursed.”

When night had come, he went away over the mountain with no possession but the torn coat on his back. At the edge of the field a hare crossed before him again, and this time he did not rebuke it.

“O Blessed Queen of Heaven,” he said, “keep me from old eagles, old fishes, old trees, old lovers, old enemies, and most of all from the old man walking within myself. And if there is no shelter from him, let my feet be light and the roads long to the end of life and time.”

Behind him the last of the thatch fell in a shower of sparks, and before him the white May blossom shone along the road.

So Owen Hanrahan became a wanderer once more.

## The Lighthouse at the End of the Street

On the morning the lighthouse appeared, Nora Vale was repairing a watch that had stopped at 3:17.

It was a silver pocket watch, heavy in her palm, with a cracked enamel face and the initials E.M. engraved on the back. Its owner, Mr. Bell, had explained that it had belonged to his father and that it had not ticked for forty-two years.

“Not since the night he disappeared,” he had added.

People often told Nora stories like that. They brought her clocks that had survived fires, watches worn through wars, music boxes that had forgotten all but three notes. They believed memory lived inside mechanisms, tucked between gears like dust. Nora never argued. She accepted each object, listened to each story, and promised only to examine the problem.

She had just removed the watch’s balance wheel when a shadow passed across her workbench.

Nora looked up.

Beyond the window of her shop, at the far end of Marrow Street, stood a lighthouse.

It rose between the bakery and the abandoned cinema, where there had always been a narrow alley blocked by two rusted bins. The tower was white, though gray weather had stained it in long vertical streaks. At its top, a glass lantern room glittered beneath a copper roof. Gulls circled around it, crying above the chimneys.

Nora set down her tweezers.

Marrow Street lay six miles inland.

For several minutes, nobody seemed to notice anything unusual. Mr. Bell sat in the chair by the door, reading yesterday’s newspaper. Across the road, Mrs. Finch arranged apples outside her grocery. A bus stopped, released three passengers, and moved on.

Then the lighthouse lamp turned once.

A pale beam swept across the street in the clear morning sun.

Mr. Bell lowered his newspaper.

“Well,” he said. “That’s new.”

By noon, half the town had gathered outside Nora’s shop. Children ran toward the tower and back again. Shopkeepers abandoned their counters. The mayor arrived wearing his ceremonial chain, though no ceremony had been announced.

The lighthouse had no door.

Its base filled the alley exactly, seamless and solid. The bakery wall touched it on one side, the cinema on the other. People knocked on the white stone, pressed their ears against it, and called upward. No one answered.

The mayor declared the structure unsafe and ordered everyone to stand back. This caused the crowd to move several inches closer.

Someone telephoned the coast guard. Someone else telephoned a newspaper. Old Mrs. Finch crossed herself and said the sea had come to collect a debt.

By sunset, the beam had begun to turn regularly. Every thirty seconds it slid over the rooftops, crossed the church steeple, flashed through windows, and vanished over the western hills.

Nora watched from her doorway.

Each time the light touched her, she smelled salt.

That night she dreamed of waves striking the sky.

The next morning, Mr. Bell returned for his watch.

“I’m afraid it isn’t finished,” Nora said. “The mainspring is sound, but something is preventing the mechanism from—”

The lighthouse lamp passed over the shop window.

The pocket watch ticked.

Once.

Mr. Bell leaned forward.

Nora stared at the watch on her bench.

At 3:17, the second hand moved.

Tick.

Tick.

Tick.

Then the beam passed on, and the watch stopped.

Neither of them spoke for a while.

At last Mr. Bell said, “Could it be magnetism?”

“Light isn’t usually magnetic.”

“Electricity?”

“There are no wires.”

“My father believed lightning could hide inside metal.”

Nora picked up the watch and turned it over. The case felt warm.

“What happened the night he disappeared?” she asked.

Mr. Bell folded his hands over the head of his cane.

“He went fishing,” he said. “At Lake Orison. A storm came in. They found his boat, but not him.”

Lake Orison was three miles north of town. It was broad and deep, but it was not the sea. It had no tides, no salt, and no need of lighthouses.

“What time was the storm?” Nora asked.

Mr. Bell looked at the watch.

“Three seventeen.”

News of the watch spread before lunch.

Soon people were bringing Nora broken clocks from every corner of town. A kitchen clock recovered from a collapsed house. A soldier’s wristwatch stopped by a bullet. A carriage clock that had frozen during a winter funeral. She placed them around the shop, and whenever the lighthouse beam crossed the windows, they came briefly alive.

Some ticked for only a second. Others rang alarms, chimed hours, or spun their hands backward. One small wooden cuckoo clock opened its door and released not a bird but the faint sound of a woman laughing.

People began to wait for the light.

They crowded into Nora’s shop, clutching heirlooms. They stood silently as the beam approached, watching its reflection travel across the opposite windows. When it entered, the room filled with ticking.

For those few seconds, the shop sounded like rain.

Then the beam moved on, and silence returned.

The newspaper called it “The Miracle of Marrow Street.” Visitors arrived from neighboring towns. Vendors sold paper lighthouses, saltwater sweets, and bottles labeled GENUINE BEAM-CAPTURED AIR. The mayor erected barriers and charged admission to the end of the street.

Nora disliked the crowds, but she could not turn away the people who came to her.

A mother brought a toy train that had belonged to her dead son. In the lighthouse beam, it traveled in a small circle, carrying no passenger.

A retired teacher brought a school bell lost for decades in his attic. When the light touched it, the bell rang, and a chorus of children’s voices recited the alphabet.

A young woman brought a watch her husband had worn when he left her. It started at once and ran perfectly even after the beam had gone. She burst into tears, though Nora could not tell whether they were tears of joy.

The objects did not all return to life, and those that did offered no clear mercy. Memory, Nora came to understand, was not a message. It was weather. It moved through people without asking what they wished to remember.

She kept one clock beneath the counter and never showed it to anyone.

It was a plain brass alarm clock with a dent near the number eight. It had belonged to her younger brother, Simon.

Twenty years earlier, when Nora was sixteen and Simon was nine, they had gone to Lake Orison on a hot August afternoon. Their mother had forbidden them to swim in the northern cove because the water there dropped suddenly into darkness.

They went anyway.

Nora remembered Simon standing on a flat rock, skinny and sunburned, pretending not to be frightened. She remembered teasing him. She remembered turning away to watch a blue dragonfly settle on her knee.

Then came the splash.

By the time she reached him, the lake had closed.

Divers searched for three days. They never found his body.

The alarm clock had been in Simon’s room, set to ring at seven on the morning after he drowned. It had never rung. Nora’s mother stopped it at 6:59 and placed it in a cupboard, where it remained until her death.

Nora had repaired thousands of clocks, but she had never opened Simon’s.

On the seventh night after the lighthouse appeared, someone knocked on her upstairs window.

Nora woke in darkness.

The knock came again.

She lived above the shop. Her bedroom window faced the lighthouse, level with rooftops but far below the lantern room. Nothing could have reached the glass.

She approached cautiously and opened the curtain.

A gull hovered outside.

Not flew—hovered. Its wings were spread but motionless. Its black eye regarded her through the pane. Around one leg was tied a strip of red cloth.

The lighthouse beam swept across the room.

The gull struck the glass with its beak.

Once.

Then it dropped from sight.

Nora opened the window and leaned out. There was no bird on the pavement below. The street was empty, silvered by moonlight. At its end, the lighthouse glowed.

For the first time, there was a door in its base.

Nora dressed quickly, took Simon’s clock from beneath the counter, and walked outside.

The night smelled strongly of salt. Fog curled around the buildings, though the sky above was clear. As Nora passed the bakery, she heard waves breaking somewhere beyond the walls.

The lighthouse door stood open.

Inside was a spiral staircase.

“Hello?” she called.

Her voice climbed the tower and came back changed, mingled with whispers.

She stepped inside.

The door closed behind her.

The staircase was iron, narrow and wet beneath her shoes. Nora began to climb, carrying the alarm clock against her chest.

At the first landing, she found Mr. Bell’s silver watch lying on a step.

She picked it up. It was ticking steadily now.

At 3:17, the staircase vanished.

For one terrible instant Nora stood in a storm. Rain struck her face. A small fishing boat pitched beneath her, and an old man clung to the mast, shouting into the wind.

“Who are you?” Nora cried.

He could not hear her.

A wave rose behind him, black and immense. The boat tipped. The old man reached inside his coat and pulled out the silver watch. He kissed it once before the water came down.

Then Nora was back on the staircase.

The watch had stopped.

She almost descended. Whatever waited above did not offer harmless visions. But Simon’s clock pressed its hard edges into her palms, and after a moment she continued.

At the second landing lay the toy train. Its wheels turned slowly.

The lighthouse opened another memory around her: a hospital room, afternoon sunlight, a boy arranging the train track across his blanket while his mother slept in a chair. The boy looked up.

Unlike Mr. Bell’s father, he saw Nora.

“Is this tomorrow?” he asked.

“No,” she whispered.

“Oh.”

He seemed disappointed.

“Do you know where the trains go when nobody’s playing with them?”

Nora shook her head.

The boy smiled. “Neither do they.”

The hospital room faded.

Nora climbed faster.

The higher she went, the more objects she found: the soldier’s wristwatch, the school bell, the carriage clock. Each one opened a moment that had been sealed inside it. A battlefield. A classroom. A snowy churchyard.

These were not ghosts. Nora understood that now. The lighthouse was not summoning the dead. It was illuminating what objects had witnessed, just as sunlight passing through glass reveals bubbles and flaws.

At last she reached the lantern room.

The great lens turned silently around a brilliant flame. Beyond the glass walls lay not the town but an ocean without horizon. Waves rolled under a starless sky. Bells rang somewhere beneath the water.

Beside the lens stood a keeper in a dark oilskin coat.

His beard was white, his face brown and deeply lined. A red cloth was tied around his left wrist.

“You took your time,” he said.

Nora recognized the cloth that had been tied to the gull.

“Who are you?”

“The keeper.”

“Of what?”

He looked toward the ocean. “Things that do not know they are lost.”

Nora held up Simon’s clock. “Can this show me my brother?”

“Yes.”

Her breath caught.

The keeper’s expression did not change.

“But that isn’t the question you climbed here to ask.”

Nora glanced at the turning light. “Why did the lighthouse come?”

“Because the town called it.”

“No one called.”

“Not aloud.”

Below them, deep in the tower, countless clocks began to strike.

The keeper walked to the glass. “For years, people here have carried unfinished hours. Moments they polish, hide, inherit, and hand down. Your town is full of time that refuses to pass.”

“And the lighthouse releases it?”

“It reveals it.”

“Why?”

“Because something must.”

Nora looked at the clock in her hands. Its minute hand rested one notch before seven.

“If I place this in the light, I’ll see what happened?”

“You already know what happened.”

“I turned away.”

“Yes.”

“Only for a moment.”

“Yes.”

“I could have saved him.”

The keeper faced her then. His eyes were pale gray, almost colorless.

“Perhaps.”

Nora had expected denial. Comfort. She had built her life around the secret hope that someone wise would one day declare her blameless.

“Perhaps?” she repeated.

“Time is not a court,” the keeper said. “It keeps no book of innocence.”

Anger rose in her. “Then what good is seeing?”

“None, sometimes.”

The lens rotated. Its light passed across Simon’s clock, and the mechanism shivered.

Nora pulled it away.

The keeper said, “You may take the memory back with you, unopened.”

“And live with not knowing?”

“You have lived with it for twenty years.”

The ocean struck the tower. The lantern room trembled.

“What happens if I look?”

“You will lose what you imagined.”

Nora stared at the clock.

For two decades, she had imagined Simon sinking into black water, reaching upward, calling her name. In some versions she almost caught his hand. In others, she never noticed he was gone. The scene changed with her guilt but always ended the same way.

She stepped into the beam.

The clock rang.

The sound was piercing, ordinary, absurd.

The lantern room disappeared.

Nora stood once more in the northern cove at Lake Orison. The sun burned gold on the water. Her sixteen-year-old self sat on the rock, watching a dragonfly. Simon stood behind her.

He did not slip.

He jumped.

Nora watched him strike the water laughing. He surfaced several yards away and splashed toward the reeds. Young Nora turned and saw empty water.

“Simon?”

Beyond the reeds, hidden from her, the boy climbed onto the muddy bank.

“Simon!”

He crouched there, grinning. He was playing a trick.

Young Nora entered the water.

The bottom dropped beneath her. She gasped, flailed, recovered, and swam farther out.

On the bank, Simon’s grin vanished.

“Nora?”

She did not hear him.

He stood. His foot slipped in the mud. He fell backward into the narrow channel beyond the reeds, where rainwater rushed toward the lake.

Nora saw his hands seize the grass.

Young Nora was still swimming in the wrong direction.

Simon tried to call, but water filled his mouth. His fingers tore lines through the mud.

Then someone stepped into the memory.

Mr. Bell’s father—the fisherman—waded through the reeds. He was younger than in the storm vision, broad-shouldered and strong. He grabbed Simon’s wrist and pulled him from the channel.

The scene shifted.

The fisherman wrapped Simon in a red blanket inside a lakeside cabin. The boy coughed water onto the floor.

“My sister,” he gasped. “She’ll think I drowned.”

The fisherman hurried toward the door, but thunder shook the cabin. Outside, rain fell in sudden gray sheets.

“Road’s washed out,” he said. “We’ll go when it clears.”

But it did not clear.

The storm lasted through the night. A landslide blocked the northern path. By morning, search parties had gathered on the southern shore while Simon slept feverishly in the cabin, hidden by forest and rain.

The memory shifted again.

Days later, the fisherman stood with Simon at a railway station in another town.

“You said you’d take me home,” Simon said.

The fisherman knelt before him. His face was bruised. “I can’t go back.”

“Why?”

There were shouts outside. Police whistles. The fisherman looked toward the door.

Only then did Nora understand. He had been running from something long before he found Simon. A crime, perhaps. A debt. A life closing behind him.

He pressed money into the boy’s hand.

“Tell the stationmaster your name. He’ll help you.”

But Simon saw officers through the window. He saw the fisherman retreat toward the tracks.

Afraid of being abandoned again, he followed.

The memory fractured into brief, bright pieces: freight trains, coastal roads, false names, cheap rooms. The fisherman became a father by accident. Simon became a boy the world believed dead.

Years passed in seconds.

Simon at twelve, repairing a radio.

Simon at seventeen, standing beside the ocean.

Simon at twenty-five, tying a strip of red cloth around the leg of an injured gull.

Simon older, bearded, climbing the stairs of a lighthouse.

Then Nora returned to the lantern room.

The keeper stood before her.

She looked at the red cloth around his wrist.

“No,” she said.

He untied it.

Beneath the cloth was a pale scar curving across his skin. Nora remembered that scar. Simon had cut himself on a broken cup when he was six. Their mother had held his hand over the sink while Nora ran for a bandage.

Nora could not move.

“You’re dead,” she whispered.

“Not yet.”

“You were alive all this time?”

“Yes.”

“Why didn’t you come home?”

Simon looked older than Mr. Bell, though he should have been only forty-nine. The lighthouse had weathered him.

“At first, I was a child and afraid. Later, I was ashamed. Then too much time had passed, and I mistook that for a reason.”

Nora struck him.

The sound cracked through the lantern room.

Simon accepted the blow without turning away.

“You let us bury an empty coffin.”

“Yes.”

“Mother died believing—”

“I know.”

“You don’t know anything.”

“I watched.”

“From where?”

“From here.”

Nora looked at the turning lens, the ocean, the impossible tower. “How long have you been in this place?”

“I found it on the coast after Elias died. Mr. Bell’s father. I came looking for shelter during a storm. The old keeper needed someone to replace him.”

“And now?”

“Now I need someone.”

Nora stepped back. “That’s why you came.”

“The lighthouse came because I asked it to.”

“You want me to stay here?”

“No. I wanted to see if you would climb.”

The flame flickered.

Simon looked suddenly exhausted.

“The lighthouse must stand where time has gathered too heavily,” he said. “When its work is done, it moves on. The keeper goes with it.”

“Then leave.”

“I can’t.”

“Why not?”

“Because I chose this instead of going home.”

The answer was so simple that Nora hated him for it.

Below, the town’s clocks began to ring again. Through the glass, the ocean faded. Rooftops emerged beneath the night. Marrow Street stretched away from the tower.

Dawn was coming.

“What happens now?” Nora asked.

“The lighthouse leaves.”

“And you?”

“With it, unless someone releases me.”

“How?”

Simon nodded toward the great flame.

At its base was a small brass door. Nora opened it. Inside, amid blue fire, she saw thousands of turning gears. In the center was an empty space shaped like a clock.

She looked at the alarm clock in her hands.

“No,” Simon said. “Not that one.”

He reached inside his coat and removed a rusted railway watch. Its face bore no hands.

“This is mine.”

Nora understood. “If I put it in the mechanism, what will happen?”

“My unfinished time will be released.”

“Will it kill you?”

“I don’t know.”

She almost laughed. After twenty years of certainty, she had climbed a lighthouse only to find more uncertainty waiting at the top.

Simon placed the watch in her palm.

It was warm.

“Do you forgive me?” he asked.

Nora closed her fingers around it.

“No.”

He nodded.

“But I don’t want you to disappear again.”

For the first time, he smiled. It was not the smile of the old keeper or the frightened runaway. It was Simon’s crooked childhood smile, the one that always seemed to expect the world to join him in some harmless crime.

“That may be enough,” he said.

Nora placed the railway watch into the empty space.

The gears caught it.

The lighthouse beam stopped.

Every clock in town struck 3:17.

The flame went out.

For an instant, Nora felt herself falling through salt, darkness, bells, and years. She reached for Simon and found his hand.

Then morning sunlight touched her face.

She was lying in the alley between the bakery and the abandoned cinema. Simon lay beside her, still holding her hand.

The lighthouse was gone.

People gathered at the alley entrance. Mr. Bell stood at the front of the crowd, leaning on his cane. He stared at Simon.

Simon slowly sat up.

From his coat came a steady ticking.

Mr. Bell’s silver watch rested in his pocket.

“Elias?” Mr. Bell asked.

Simon shook his head.

But he rose, crossed the alley, and placed the watch in the old man’s hand.

“Your father saved my life,” he said.

Around them, the town was quiet. The broken clocks had stopped again. The toy train stood still. The school bell held its silence. Whatever memories the light had opened were sealed once more.

Yet not everything returned to what it had been.

Mrs. Finch claimed she could hear gulls whenever rain approached. The mayor stopped wearing his ceremonial chain. The young woman whose husband had left sold her watch and bought a railway ticket west.

Mr. Bell’s pocket watch continued to run.

So did Simon’s alarm clock.

It rang every morning at seven in the apartment above Nora’s shop, where Simon slept on a folding bed by the window. Some mornings Nora hated the sound. Some mornings she hated him. Forgiveness did not arrive like a lighthouse beam, brilliant and complete. It came by degrees: a cup of tea left outside a door, a shared joke, an argument survived.

Simon learned to repair clocks.

He was not very good at it. He lost screws, bent springs, and insisted on humming while he worked. Customers sometimes found him staring toward the end of the street, where the narrow alley had returned.

Years later, when people asked Nora whether the lighthouse had truly existed, she gave the same answer she gave to anyone who asked if a ruined watch could be repaired.

“Bring it to me,” she said. “I’ll see what can be done.”

And on certain nights, when fog filled Marrow Street and the windows smelled faintly of salt, a pale beam passed over the rooftops.

It never stayed.

But in the shop below, every clock remembered how to tick.
